```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
library(geosphere)
set.seed(222)
theme_set(theme_bw(22))

soil_cores <- read_csv("data/exide-soil-cores.csv") |>
  filter(pb_ppm <= 5e3)

ena_esa <- soil_cores |>
  mutate(area = str_sub(property_id, 1, 3)) |>
  filter(area %in% c("ENA", "ESA")) |>
  mutate(area2 = ifelse(area == "ENA", 0, 1)) |>
  slice_sample(n = 40, by = area)

# Approximate location of the former Exide facility (2700 S Indiana St, Vernon)
exide_lon <- -118.1923
exide_lat <- 34.0058

soil_cores <- read_csv("data/exide-soil-cores.csv") |>
  filter(location_code == "YD", pb_ppm <= 5e3) |>
  mutate(
    distance_ft = distGeo(cbind(longitude, latitude), c(exide_lon, exide_lat)) *
      3.28,
    distance_mi = distance_ft / 5280,
    bearing_deg = bearing(c(exide_lon, exide_lat), cbind(longitude, latitude))
  ) |>
  drop_na()

step_out <- read_csv("data/step-out.csv") |>
  mutate(distance_mi = distance_ft / 5280)

all_samples_north <- bind_rows(
  `soil core` = transmute(
    filter(soil_cores, between(bearing_deg, 0, 30)),
    property_id,
    distance_ft,
    distance_mi,
    pb_ppm
  ),
  `step out` = select(step_out, property_id, distance_ft, distance_mi, pb_ppm),
  .id = "source"
) |>
  drop_na()
```

# Categorical predictors

## Learning objectives

- **Visualize** relationships with a _categorical predictor_
- **Model** relationships with a _categorical predictor_
- **Implement** a _categorical predictor_ in `lm()`

# Visualize relationships with a _categorical predictor_

## Two continuous variables

Here, a regression line describes the relationship between two continuous variables.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(all_samples_north, aes(x = distance_mi, y = pb_ppm)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    color = "cornflowerblue",
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  labs(x = "Distance (mi)", y = "Soil Pb (ppm)")
```

## Continuous ~ categorical

Regression can represent more types of relationships, such as a continuous response to categorical predictor.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center

ena_esa_lm <- lm(pb_ppm ~ area, data = ena_esa)
ena_esa_plot <- ggplot(ena_esa, aes(x = area2, y = pb_ppm)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, seed = 222),
    shape = 21,
    fill = "cornflowerblue",
    color = "white",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = coef(ena_esa_lm)[1],
    slope = coef(ena_esa_lm)[2],
    color = "grey50",
    linewidth = 2
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:1, labels = c("ENA", "ESA")) +
  labs(x = "Area", y = "Soil Pb (ppm)")
ena_esa_plot
```

## What's the "value" of $x$?

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

What is the value of $x$? $\beta_1 \times \text{ENA}$ doesn't make sense...

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center

ena_esa_plot
```

# Model relationships with a _categorical predictor_

## Treat categories as 0's and 1's

::: {.columns}

::: {.column style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

When `area` is "ENA", let $x=0$

$$
\begin{align}
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x \\
y &= \beta_0
\end{align}
$$

:::

::: {.column style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

When `area` is "ESA", let $x=1$

$$
\begin{align}
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x \\
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1
\end{align}
$$



:::

:::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center

ena_esa_plot +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:1, labels = c("0\nENA", "1\nESA"))
```

## Recode your _levels_

Conceptually, here's what happens:

:::{style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
- `area` was a category with two **_levels_**.
- Pick one level as the **_reference_** ("ENA").
- Create a **_dummy variable_** for the other level.
:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

This...

```{r}
ena_esa |>
  slice(1:3, .by = area) |>
  select(area, pb_ppm) |>
  head()
```

:::

::: {.column}

...becomes this

```{r}
ena_esa |>
  slice(1:3, .by = area) |>
  transmute(ESA = as.integer(area == "ESA"), pb_ppm) |>
  head()
```

:::

:::

## New interpretations for $\beta$s

With two continuous variables, $\beta_0$ is the **_intercept_** and $\beta_1$ is the **_slope_**.

Look at the statistical notation and the visualization. What do the $\beta$s mean now?

## Reference and difference, equation

::: {.columns}

::: {.column style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

What is the _expected_ value ($y$) when `area` is "ENA" ($x=0$)?

$$
\begin{align}
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x \\
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 0 \\
y &= \beta_0
\end{align}
$$

:::

::: {.column style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

What is the _expected_ value ($y$) when `area` is "ESA" ($x=1$)?

$$
\begin{align}
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x \\
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 1 \\
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1
\end{align}
$$

:::

:::

$\beta_0$ is now the expected (mean) value of the _reference level_ (ENA here).

$\beta_1$ is the _difference_ between its level (ESA) and the reference level.

## Reference and difference, visualized

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-align: center

dx <- 0.25
betas <- coef(ena_esa_lm)
ena_esa_means <- tibble(
  x1 = 0:1 - dx,
  x2 = 0:1 + dx,
  y = c(betas[1], sum(betas))
)

ena_esa_betas <- tibble(
  x = c(0, 0.5, 1),
  y1 = c(0, betas[1], 0),
  y2 = c(betas[1], sum(betas), sum(betas)),
  y3 = (y1 + y2) / 2,
  beta = expression(beta[0], beta[1], beta[0] + beta[1])
)
ena_esa_plot_betas <- ggplot(ena_esa, aes(x = area2, y = pb_ppm)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, seed = 222),
    shape = 21,
    fill = "cornflowerblue",
    color = "white",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x1, xend = x2, y = y, yend = y),
    ena_esa_means,
    color = "grey50",
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x, xend = x, y = y1, yend = y2),
    ena_esa_betas,
    arrow = arrow(),
    color = "grey50",
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(x = x, y = y3, label = beta),
    ena_esa_betas,
    hjust = 0,
    nudge_x = 0.05
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:1, labels = c("ENA", "ESA")) +
  labs(x = "Area", y = "Soil Pb (ppm)")
ena_esa_plot_betas
```

# Implement a _categorical predictor_ in `lm()`


# Recap

## Categorical predictors

::: {.incremental}
- Linear regression can model the relationship between a continuous response (e.g., soil lead concentrations) and a _**categorical predictor**_ (e.g., areas ENA and ESA).
- One _**level**_ becomes the _**reference**_ (e.g., ENA).
- The interpretation of the coefficients changes.
  - $\beta_0$ becomes the _**mean of the reference level**_.
  - $\beta_1$ becomes the _**difference between levels**_.
- The call to `lm()` is _**unchanged**_.
  - _How cool is that??_
:::

## Interpretation

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-align: center
ena_esa_plot_betas
```
